articles.title: Canadian professor warns massive new data center would release ‘23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy’ every day
articles.content: Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary’s Wonder Valley data center plans are under scrutiny The Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) has filed for a judicial review over the project, which is planned to be the world’s largest data center A physicist hired by the SLCN has declared the data center will release significant heat waste A physicist acting on behalf of the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) has claimed that the O’Leary Digital Wonder Valley data center would release “23 atomic bombs of energy” while adding that the declaration is “a first-order estimate intended to convey scale.” The report by Utah State University physicist Robert Davies, working on behalf of the SLCN, whose lawyer, also adds that current regulations for developing land are not suited to projects of the data center’s scale. O’Leary Digital Wonder Valley, plans for which were first unveiled in 2024, was conceived to be the largest on the planet when completed, and has a $70 billion budget for the 64 square kilometer (almost 15815 acres) development. Its planned location is in the SLCN’s traditional territory in Alberta, Canada. First-order estimate The planned scale of the data center, earmarked for a location 130 km southwest of the SLCN’s reserve, is the main point of contention, and the basis for Professor Robert Davies, of the Utah State University. But his claim over the “23 atomic bombs of energy” demands some clarification. "Now of course, that’s not explosions, but that’s just trying to get a sense of how much energy we’re talking about,” said Davies in the assessment. “The effect will almost certainly be large, if not extreme.” He also notes that “every quantitative figure … should be treated as a first-order estimate intended to convey scale, to be confirmed against the developer's own filings.” Davies also highlights that the project could be “the largest single-site heat source on the entire planet.” The assessment, which was prepared for SLCN’s case, emphasizes that it is “not a comprehensive environmental review, a formal expert report, or a legal opinion.” Robust regulatory process While Davies’ contribution to the SLCN’s judicial review filing relies on further information from O’Leary Digital, it paints a worrying picture, not least into the effects of the heat waste on the surrounding wildlife. "I can't imagine allowing it to go forward without those full assessments,” Davies said, while also criticizing the use of traditional environmental legislation and guidelines for giant data center projects. “When people talk about environmental regulations that these projects have to adhere to, those regulations were not created with anything of this scale in mind.” Naturally, O’Leary Digital has responded to the filing. CEO Paul Palandjian wrote in an email “We also respect the robust and stringent regulatory process we must follow in advancing Wonder Valley… we’re having productive dialogue with Indigenous communities through consultation and engagement, and we remain committed to that work."
articles.author: Christian Cawley
articles.fingerprint: atomic bombs canadian center data day energy every hiroshima massive professor release sized warns worth would

articles.title: I spent a morning with Meta VR Glasses and wish I never had to take them off
articles.content: Experience counts for something, and nowhere is that more evident than on the Meta VR Glasses I finally wore this morning. These lightweight, intuitive, and engrossing VR glasses shed the weight and overdesigned fussiness of previous VR and mixed reality headsets to deliver a subtle, smart, eminently comfortable and fun wearable experience that is equally at home entertaining you with wild VR movies or expansive, productivity-enhancing virtual desktops. Granted, my walkthrough of the $1,299 VR Glasses that are expected to arrive next spring (April-early June) of next year was a breezy 45 minutes, but that was ample time to realize that Meta VR Glasses were truly built on all the lessons of not only Meta Quest VR, but also by watching competitors like Apple and even Samsung struggle to inspire consumers with stunning but also expensive or somewhat unwieldy mixed reality experiences. Lance Ulanoff / Future Lance Ulanoff / Future Lance Ulanoff / Future Lance Ulanoff / Future In my view, Meta's decision to move compute, storage, and battery out of the headset and into a 300g belt- or pocket-friendly puck pays design dividends. The wearable, which looks like a slightly oversized pair of sunglasses, is so comfortable that I barely felt them on my face, and after 45 minutes of continuous use, I didn't remove the 100-gram frames with a sense of relief. If anything, I was sad my all-too-brief interlude was over. Without needing to support CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, RAM, a heavy battery, or even SD storage, Meta could focus on basic aesthetic appeal. The Meta VR Glasses feel and look spare, but in a positive way. By design, they do not cut you off from the outside world (there will be an optional light shield), so there's no need to slap a pair of animated blinking eyes on the lenses. Granted, I had my doubts that the Meta VR Glasses would be all that immersive or inspiring, given what looked like essentially eye-sized lenses and no visible cameras, inside or out. That all turned out to be deceiving. Accurate tracking for an immersive experience (Image credit: Lance Ulanoff / Future) When I said Meta clearly learned from all that came before it, I wasn't kidding. The metaphors for setting up eye tracking were essentially the same as what I did for Apple Vision Pro (I didn't have to adjust pupillary distance, though you easily can) and, to an extent, Galaxy XR. You look at a circle of dots floating in space and, yes, use your fingers to pinch and select each one. There are, obviously, cameras that track your eyes, hands, and the outside world. I was impressed with the accuracy, which matched what I've experienced on Vision Pro. Equally, the first time I saw the floating menu, I was shocked at the visual quality (it's worth noting that Meta put in a pair of magnetic prescription inserts to match my eyes, and those inserts will probably add $150 to your final cost). For the record, Meta lists the Micro-OLED display resolution as 5K, and based on what I saw, I believe it. Disney+, a TV App, Avengers: Infinity War VR experience, and a dozen other app icons floated in space, with each one puffing up as I glanced at it. (Image credit: Lance Ulanoff / Future) Meta VR Glasses software doesn't try to reinvent the mixed reality wheel. I had no trouble opening apps, closing them, or even moving windows around. It does add one gesture that I appreciated: scroll. To scroll in any window, I made a gentle fist and then swiped my thumb across the side of my index finger to scroll left, right, up, and down. I was surprised at how quickly I picked this up; I think that has a lot to do with the accuracy of the eye and gesture tracking. My experiences were limited to a handful of apps, but each one was compelling in its own way. (Image credit: Meta) We started with an 8K VR Billie Eilish concert in which I was virtually seated front and center, close enough to take a selfie with the singer. The volume started a bit low for my tastes. Still, I was able to use the…

articles.title: X says its updated web app is way faster
articles.content: X is introducing a new version of its web app that it says is much faster than before, and it's now rolling out the updated app "one country at a time" for signed-in users. "Open a profile on X.com over a slow connection," principal engineer Yagiz Nizipli said in a blog post about the changes. "On the old web app, you'd stare at the X logo for more than 22 seconds before the first post appeared. On the new one, it shows up in 2.7." The post also goes into technical detail about how the updated app "replaces the three servers we used to run for people, search crawlers, and link previews with one." articles.title: Hands on: Siri Recaps & Live Rewind are controversial & unnecessary technologies
articles.content: After spending a day with Apple's Audio Intelligence features, they feel more like checked boxes than fully realized and useful features in spite of the clear privacy and boundaries present. Siri Recap and Live Rewind are odd features for Apple to offer When Apple first revealed Siri Recaps and Live Rewind during its September event, there was a lot of confusion and concern around the features . Now that they can be tested with the iOS 27.3 beta, I can say they are complicated to say the least. Siri Recaps will listen while you're in a specific location, like work, or during a certain period of time you've set. Users can have it active all day if they wish. articles.title: Apple Releases Safari Technology Preview 256 With Bug Fixes and Performance Improvements
articles.content: Apple today released a new update for Safari Technology Preview , the experimental browser that was first introduced in March 2016. Apple designed ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ to allow users to test features that are planned for future release versions of the Safari browser. ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ 256 includes fixes and updates for Accessibility, Animations, CSS, Editing, Forms, HTML, JavaScript, Media, Networking, Rendering, SVG, Security, Web API, Web Extensions, Web Inspector, WebGL, and WebRTC. The current ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ release is compatible with machines running macOS Tahoe and macOS Golden Gate , the newest version of macOS. The ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ update is available through the Software Update mechanism in System Preferences or System Settings to anyone who has downloaded the browser from Apple's website. Complete release notes for the update are available on the Safari Technology Preview website . Apple's aim with ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ is to gather feedback from developers and users on its browser development process. ‌Safari Technology Preview‌ can run side-by-side with the existing Safari browser and while it is designed for developers, it does not require a developer account to download and use. articles.title: Apps Can Now Try to Stop You From Canceling Subscriptions
articles.content: Apple today added a new subscription retention feature for developers, allowing them to show retention messages when a subscriber goes to cancel. Apple says retention messages will appear in the subscription cancellation flow and can include text, images, or a special offer. Retention messages can be added in App Store Connect for auto-renewable subscriptions, with options for subscriber eligibility and wait time between messages. Through a separate Retention Messaging API, developers can choose which messages to show a subscriber based on their subscription details. API access is by request. ‌App Store‌ users may see offers for discounts or reasons to keep a subscription before canceling. articles.title: Tiny's new AI workstation is anything but — packing in 16 TB SSD array and 128 GB GPU memory, but with an eye-watering price tag to boot
articles.content: Tiny Corp's $30,000 tinybox Red Kimi pairs four Radeon AI Pro R9700 GPUs (128 GB GDDR6) with sixteen 1 TB NVMe SSDs A tinygrad driver lets the GPUs read the 238.4 GB/s SSD array directly to run Moonshot's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 Tiny claims 40 tokens per second, but the math involves caching nearly all of each token's weights in VRAM There is nothing tiny about Tiny Corp's latest tinybox, the tinybox Red Kimi: It costs a mammoth $30,000 and pairs four AMD Radeon AI Pro R9700 graphics cards with sixteen 1 TB NVMe SSDs, all with one goal in mind: running Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 on a desk rather than in a data center. Each R9700 carries 32 GB of GDDR6 at 640 GB/s, giving the four cards 128 GB of GPU memory and 2,560 GB/s of aggregate bandwidth to go with a system built on Tiny Corp's G5 platform, with a 32-core AMD Epyc Genoa processor whose exact model the tinybox configurator doesn't name, and a modest 32 GB of DDR5 system memory in tow. Tiny Corp claims the machine can run Kimi K3 at 40 tokens per second, a figure nobody outside the company has tested yet. Sixteen drives, four GPUs and an AMD EPYC CPU rule the roost The storage in play is the unique selling point for Tiny Corp's behemoth: its 16 drives form a RAID array rated at 238.4 GB/s, and Tiny Corp says its tinygrad software now includes a driver that lets the AMD GPUs control the NVMe drives directly, rather than routing every read through the CPU. Sharing the system's topology on X , the company pitched the result as "frontier models at home at usable speeds for a good price." The rationale comes down to capacity. Moonshot's model card shows Kimi K3 ships with native MXFP4 weights, and Hyperstack measured the published checkpoint at roughly 1.56 TB. The four GPUs can hold about 8% of that, so the rest has to live somewhere, and Tiny Corp has picked considerably cheaper flash over DRAM. The concept isn't entirely new: Researchers from Nvidia and the University of Illinois presented GPU-initiated SSD access in the BaM system architecture at ASPLOS 2023, treating storage as another tier of accelerator memory. Tiny Corp's offering, however, is a working version on AMD workstation cards, inside a box you can actually order. The configurator's own code estimates the Red Kimi's installed weight at around 56 pounds, in a chassis 12 inches wide, 19.25 inches tall, and 18 inches deep. It also raises the noise rating from under 50 dB to under 60 dB for R9700 builds, warning that the cards' blower fans are "audible". Kimi K3 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates 16 of its 896 routed experts, plus two shared experts, for 104 billion active parameters per token. At MXFP4's effective 4.25 bits per weight, that means reading at least 55 GB of weights for every token generated. If every one of those bytes were read from the SSDs, the array would manage only about four tokens per second. Reaching 40 tokens per second means moving roughly 2.2 TB/s of weights, about 86% of the four GPUs' combined memory bandwidth, while the SSDs could contribute at most about 6 GB per token, or around 11% of what each one needs. In a nutshell, the claim only works if the GPUs' 128 GB already contains nearly everything each token touches, even though it fits less than a tenth of the model. That is achievable if expert selection is predictable enough to cache well, or if Tiny Corp is running a lower-precision quantization than Moonshot's native format, speculative decoding, or a mix of the three. Tiny Corp hasn't published the precision, context length, batch size, or method behind its number, and it would be prudent to treat it as a manufacturer claim at best. The aggregate bandwidth figure also assumes the workload is split evenly across four cards that communicate over PCIe. A pricey proposition that goes neck and neck with Apple's Mac Studio At $30,000, the Red Kimi is a lot of money for a desktop computer, but the alternatives for running a 2.8-trillion-parameter…

articles.title: Building AI factories at enterprise scale
articles.content: AI has become a juggernaut, driving technical strategy in the tech sector and outside of it. With the worldwide server market growing 30 percent in a single year to hit $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025, IDC now feels safe recategorizing AI-driven investment "from cyclical to durable". The analyst company expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year, adding that it's growing fastest at the edge. Why enterprises are building their own All this investment in AI infrastructure might once have come mainly for hyperscalers, but that's changing quickly. Adoption is spreading quickly beyond public cloud service providers into enterprise environments, IDC adds. They're eager to run agentic AI in-house. There are plenty of reasons for companies to own their own AI infrastructure rather than offloading it to the cloud. One of these is data control, especially in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and the public sector that have sovereign data requirements. Another revolves around the need for predictable costing from tokens delivered on tunable in-house systems. So what should companies look for in a supplier? Delivery speed will be a powerful driver for many who are under the gun to deliver AI initiatives for the business, especially during periods of constrained memory and CPU supply. Life cycle services will also come near the top of the list, for companies that need help managing everything from the power through to the reasoning LLM models and the workloads that use them. That need for expertise is unlikely to stop; companies will undergo changes in AI strategy as they get to grips with a still-evolving technology. From the desk to the datacenter ASUS expects this AI surge to continue in the datacenter, but elsewhere too, specifically in edge locations (especially industrial use cases) and at developers' desks, as the applications that will power the enterprise get made. It wants to be top of peoples' list for hardware and services at all these places along the AI continuum. At NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on Oct 21-22, it announced a full-stack AI offering that it's calling its Enterprise Agentic AI Solution . It's three-layer affair, featuring: ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure: Its selection of AI servers, including several new units. ASUS AI Software Stack: Its software for integrating and controlling AI workflows. ASUS AI HUB: A services operation that ties it all together. These bring together some existing assets that ASUS had for enterprise AI users, along with some new ones. The time is right for an end-to-end offering with new hardware because of the way the market is shifting, say ASUS execs. "ASUS servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure capable of supporting both complex task execution and large-scale AI agent deployment, accelerating enterprise adoption of agentic AI," says Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS. While generative AI initially spiked demand, the advent of agentic AI has sent compute demand into overdrive. Ju explains that the focus is expanding from the GPU. "Historically, AI servers have been optimized primarily around GPU compute. But as enterprise AI shifts toward agentic AI, workloads increasingly revolve around a continuous ‘agent loop’ that is heavily CPU-dependent," he says. That loop takes in task planning, code execution, external tool invocation, and reflection or correction work. The CPU's increased role in this execution work is creating bottlenecks in conventional AI servers, he adds. The first such sticking point is single-thread performance, which leaves GPUs idling while they wait for CPUs to complete. The second lies in memory bandwidth. When this is managed on a per-core basis, it can slow things down when many agents run at once. The multi-die design of many CPUs also penalizes them in AI environments, because accessing data across dies…

I’m glad I managed to fluke myself home, as TEARDROP-SHAPED THINGS completely eluded me; I had no idea what a UVULA was and thought SPEEDBAG was just a smaller version of a punchball. And as for PEAR — surely that’s pear-shaped, rather than teardrop-shaped? NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the New York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult. On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a process of elimination. What's more, you can make up to four mistakes, which gives you a little bit of breathing room. It's a little more involved than something like Wordle, however, and there are plenty of opportunities for the game to trip you up with tricks. articles.title: Axon Sued Over AI-Powered License Plate Reader Network
articles.content: Axon has been sued in a proposed class action accusing the Taser and police body-camera maker of illegally collecting and storing license plate data on millions of California drivers through its AI-powered surveillance network. Reuters reports the details: - The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Tuesday in federal court in San Francisco by law firms Hausfeld and Gibbs Mura, alleges Axon has failed to comply with a California privacy provision by not disclosing how it collects, uses and shares plate data gathered through its camera systems - "Axon has created a mass-surveillance infrastructure that is practically impossible to avoid," the lawsuit said - Scottsdale, Arizona-based Axon did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit said the company has more than 1,000 cameras in California and alleges millions of drivers may have been affected - Some Axon cameras are installed in high-traffic areas and collect plate information as vehicles pass by. Other cameras are placed inside police vehicles, the lawsuit said - The proposed class covers drivers whose vehicle plate information was captured by an automated license plate reader in California and processed or stored by Axon's system since 2023 - The lawsuit seeks more than $5 million in damages, in addition to a court order stopping Axon from its allegedly unlawful practices Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product
articles.content: Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh unveils vsActual, an AI product that customers can use without Smartsheet, during his keynote at the company’s Engage conference in Seattle on Wednesday. (GeekWire Photo / Todd Bishop) Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet. The Bellevue, Wash.-based company unveiled vsActual , as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course. It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users. At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box. “Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone. Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule. Raj Singh speaks at Smartsheet Engage in downtown Seattle on Wednesday. (GeekWire Photo / Todd Bishop) In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product. “Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.” Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work. It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp. Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020 . All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said. “The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said. vsActual compares a project’s plan against what’s happening in Slack, Workday, Jira and Smartsheet, flagging a launch that has slipped nine weeks even though two of the systems still show it on track. (Smartsheet Image) A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available. Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long. articles.title: 'Super Mario Odyssey' Can Now Run on Apple TV Thanks to AI
articles.content: A Reddit user was able to get Nintendo's "Animal Crossing: New Horizons" and "Super Mario Odyssey" to run natively on the Apple TV 4K , continuing a string of ports made possible with the use of AI (via Engadget ). TVPort , Reddit user FloatingFalafel's open-source project, is a fork of the nxnative toolkit used to recompile Switch and Switch 2 games for the Apple TV using a Mac. It was built using Claude Opus 5.5. "Super Mario Odyssey" runs at 60fps according to FloatingFalafel, and "Animal Crossing" runs at 30fps. Other games haven't been tested, but the creator says people are welcome to use the open-source software to get other games to run. Game files are not included, and users will need to supply files from their own game cartridges, which requires a modified Nintendo Switch. [Release] TVPort - Port switch games to run natively on AppleTV (4k 3rd gen) by u/FloatingFalafel in decomps More intensive games like "The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom" may not be able to run on the third-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K because of thermal throttling. The fourth-generation ‌Apple TV‌ 4K that launches November 13 may be able to run titles the third-generation model can't. Nintendo often takes issue with unofficial ways to play its games, so TVPort may not survive long. In 2024, Nintendo sued the Yuzu emulator team , and the lawsuit led to a $2.4 million settlement and the sunsetting of the emulator. articles.title: SteelSeries Rival Pro Mini review: S-tier performance in a compact package
articles.content: SteelSeries Rival Pro Mini review The SteelSeries Rival Pro Mini might just be perfect for you, if you're looking for a compact gaming mouse that makes no sacrifices when it comes to performance. The SteelSeries Rival Pro Mini has everything a competitive gamer could ever want, be that true 8K polling, programmable buttons, 42K DPI sensitivity… you name it. It even brings ‘infinite power supply’ tech to the table, meaning you’ll have next to no downtime when duking it out against your opponents. However, this mouse doesn’t come cheap. At $179.99 / £169.99 (about AU$250), it sits firmly in the premium category, meaning it has to go above and beyond to prove itself against the best mice on the market. But is it truly worth that steep asking price? Here’s my view after hours of intensive testing. Let’s start things off by looking at some of the features that the Rival Pro Mini has to offer. I may have piqued your curiosity when I mentioned that ‘infinite’ power supply just now — but what exactly does that mean? Well, the Rival Pro Mini and its accompanying Ultra Wideband base station come with hot-swappable batteries. One will slot into your mouse while gaming, and the other will sit in the base station and charge up in the meantime. When your mouse eventually runs dry — around 60 hours with 1K polling or 16 hours with 8K — you can simply pop the battery out of your base station, slot it into your mouse, and continue playing in an instant. This is a truly brilliant feature, and means you’ll never run out of juice when competing in a tournament or playing a few casual rounds. Even though the Rival Pro Mini mouse has no USB slot for wired use, this tech means that you’ll never truly need it. But there are so many more features to discover on the Rival Pro Mini. First up, you’re getting true 8K polling for ultra-smooth performance. SuperSync is also here, which enables you to independently set tracking and clicking polling rates. There’s also aim tools, 42K DPI sensitivity, and six fully programmable buttons on board. You can customize the way that buttons function in the GG app or web platform, which also lets you adjust sensitivity, polling rate, and power management among other things. I found both the downloadable and web app to be incredibly easy to use and navigate, with no shortage of options at my disposal. (Image credit: Future) But just how does the Rival Pro Mini feel to use in practice? Just as good as you’d hope. When playing Cyberpunk 2077 on the LG UltraGear 25G590B 1000Hz gaming monitor , I was blown away by the all-round quality on offer. When aiming, movement felt supremely stable and accurate, and even basic functions like turning the camera was super smooth and highly responsive. In addition, the optical switches had a great feel to them, and allowed me to blast down my foes with unrivaled speed and precision. Like typical optical switches, these aren’t the quietest around, but their satisfying click felt never seemed obnoxiously loud or distracting to me. The mechanical scroll wheel also impressed me with its control and tactility, and its ridges provided ample grip when gaming or simply performing everyday tasks at work. This mouse gets it right when it comes to ergonomics too, although it is a more compact model, so if you have larger hands I’d recommend picking up the full-sized Rival Pro instead. But the mouse’s molded exterior and lightweight feel fantastic, and I was able to use the Rival Pro Mini for hours on end without any cramp or fatigue. This is an ergonomic model for right-handed gamers, though, so if you’re a lefty, I’d suggest checking out the symmetrical SteelSeries Sensei Pro Mini. The Rival Pro Mini plays it fairly safe looks-wise, but it does have a sleek aesthetic, and the orange scroll wheel gives it a bit of pop. It also has strong build quality, and I liked its lightly textured matte finish, which adds a premium touch. One thing I will say, however, is that this finish does turn the Rival…

articles.title: OpenAI Says ChatGPT Is Catching Up to Google In Search
articles.content: Adam Fry, OpenAI's consumer product lead for ChatGPT, says the number of searches performed through ChatGPT has grown to roughly 20% of Google's search volume. The company defines a search as a ChatGPT query that triggers a web search, suggesting the chatbot is becoming an increasingly significant competitor to traditional search engines. The Verge reports: Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google's 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it -- now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) As for ads, which OpenAI started testing earlier this year, Fry said they haven't produced a lasting backlash. "Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product," he said, adding that "most people do not seem to mind ads in the product." Last month, OpenAI announced plans to introduce images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Anthropic found a way to prove which AI model answered you — but there’s a costly catch
articles.content: Developers using AI APIs have little way of knowing whether the model answering their requests is actually the one they’re paying for. A provider could route requests to a cheaper model, or an attacker could interfere with responses, without customers having an obvious way to detect the switch. Now, Anthropic wants to change that. The company’s Frontier Red Team has released FlashProve , an open-source cryptographic system designed to verify which AI model produced a response without exposing its underlying weights. Announced Tuesday , the research could eventually help developers verify third-party AI services and detect compromised inference systems. But FlashProve remains a research prototype, and the cost of generating proofs makes it impractical for routine API traffic. But FlashProve remains a research prototype, and the cost of generating proofs makes it impractical for routine API traffic. How FlashProve proves the model FlashProve uses zkSNARKs to verify that a response came from a specific set of model weights without revealing those weights. The commitment still has to come from a trusted source, or the proof means little. Anthropic has released FlashProve on GitHub , where developers can download the code and test the system themselves. It’s still a research prototype, however, and isn’t available as a feature of the Claude API. The cost of every proof Anthropic tested FlashProve on Meta’s Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, rather than Claude. According to Anthropic’s benchmarks , FlashProve processed roughly 110 prompt tokens per second while generating proofs on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each proof was about 18.78 MB and took around 21 seconds to verify on a single CPU thread. Generating the proof is far more expensive than checking it. Compared with standard inference using vLLM, FlashProve needed 70 to 95 times more GPU time to generate proofs. It also generates them in batches after requests are completed, rather than verifying tokens as they’re delivered. FlashProve cuts proof sizes to roughly 19 MB and verification times to seconds FlashProve cuts proof sizes to roughly 19 MB and verification times to seconds, although generating those proofs remains expensive and less practical for applications that need immediate verification of every response. For developers already watching every token of their inference spend , adding that much GPU overhead would be difficult to justify for routine API traffic. Still, Anthropic says FlashProve is substantially faster than previous open-source systems. An earlier system called VerInf needed 14.3 hours to generate a proof covering 1,000 tokens. The resulting proof was 93.6 GB and took almost a day to verify. Claude built it, humans verified Anthropic credits Claude with much of FlashProve’s development, including optimizations that made its cryptographic proofs substantially faster. But the researchers still had to verify that those improvements hadn’t compromised the protocol’s security guarantees. The team used Lean to formally verify the protocol’s mathematical properties, including that it accepts valid proofs, rejects forged proofs with overwhelming probability, and doesn’t reveal the model’s weights beyond what the responses disclose. FlashProve includes two verifiers: a faster C++ implementation and a Lean version backed by formal proofs. The C++ verifier passed Anthropic’s comparison tests, but it hasn’t been formally verified. Neither has the GPU prover. Anthropic says the C++ verifier and GPU prover have been tested against the formally defined protocol, but neither has the same mathematical guarantees as the Lean implementation. Why FlashProve isn’t production-ready FlashProve is still limited to 1,024 tokens of context. articles.title: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
articles.content: For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM , SSDs , and GPUs . Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges. Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance . That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges. That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips. articles.title: What Happens When the Model Reads It Wrong: Building LLM Compliance Review That Survives an Audit
articles.content: AML work teaches you early that the two kinds of compliance mistakes don't cost the same. A false alert costs an analyst an afternoon, while a missed violation can end up in a regulator's findings. I learned that while writing regulatory modules for a banking client in 2014, and it was still on my mind years later at Capital One, when my teams built AI-enabled OCR and LLM workflows for compliance review. Those workflows reduced manual review effort by about 60%. Most of our engineering time went into the cases where the model misread a document and what the system should do next. Twenty Years of Reading Rules for a Living I didn't come to this through machine learning. My first decade was integration and data work: messaging systems, a payment-messaging gateway migration at a bank in Melbourne, and later AML scenario logic built on top of enterprise data marts. Years of that work showed me how many processes in a bank depend on someone reading a document and checking it against a rule. At Capital One, I spent several years scaling Auto Navigator, a customer-facing lending platform, from a pilot to more than a million monthly users. Between 2021 and 2023, I led engineering teams modernizing auto-lending and compliance platforms, and that's where the OCR and LLM work happened. Along the way, I was lead inventor on a patent (US10867268B1) for applying AI to external regulatory and enforcement information to spot emerging compliance risk. I was used to machines reading regulatory text; letting one make the call on a document was new. Why Compliance Review Is a Hard Place for an LLM The error asymmetry is the first problem, and it breaks the metric most teams reach for. A system can be 97% accurate overall and still miss the violations you care about, because the aggregate number blends easy passes with the rare failures that matter. Precision and recall per rule, with recall on violations treated as the number that can block a release, tell you whether the system is safe to ship. The second problem is that every decision has to be explainable after the fact. An auditor can pick any cleared document from last year and ask why it was cleared. "The model was confident" won't satisfy an examiner. You need to trace each decision to the exact text it relied on and the system version that made it. There's also a calendar problem that engineers tend to underestimate. In a regulated company, customer documents can't go to an arbitrary endpoint, so model hosting, logging, and data handling all go through security and compliance review before anyone tests on real data. In my experience, that review can take longer than building the prototype, and plans that leave no room for it slip. The Prototype Everyone Builds First It looks good in a demo. You pick a dozen clean documents, the model returns sensible verdicts with nicely written reasoning, and the room gets excited. It also hides almost everything that will go wrong in production, which is why any pipeline like this should run in shadow mode beside human reviewers before it decides anything. Where That Prototype Breaks Extraction Loss: Scanned documents carry stamps, signatures, skewed pages, faded print, and multi-column layouts. OCR on those pages doesn't fail loudly. It drops a line, merges two columns, or misreads a number, and passes along text that is mostly right. The model has no way to know a clause is missing, so it reasons carefully over an incomplete document. The mistake is treating OCR output as ground truth when nothing downstream carries a signal about extraction quality. Rationales You Can't Check: Ask a broad question and accept free-text reasoning, and some of what comes back will cite clauses that aren't in the document, or paraphrase loosely enough that a reviewer can't find the source sentence. The verdict may even be right. For an audit trail that doesn't help, because nobody can show where it came from. The Long Tail: Test sets get built from the most common…

articles.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.content: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data. Wielding DarkSword One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one that added malicious JavaScript into it. articles.title: webAI Releases TwIL-8B, an 8.8B Reasoning Model Scoring 98.2 on MATH-500
articles.content: webAI has released TwIL-8B , an 8.8B reasoning model for math, code and instruction following. The TwIL-8B reasoning model is post-trained from IBM’s Granite 4.2 8B . Weights are on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. webAI’s launch post frames the pitch around cost per task, not raw scale. The 4-bit build is 4.98 GiB, sized for CPU or modest-VRAM GPU inference. TL;DR Size: 8.79B parameters, dense. 131,072-token context, inherited from the base model. Runs on: CPU or modest-VRAM GPU via a 4.98 GiB Q4_K_M GGUF. Full bf16 weights are 16.38 GiB. Performance: Leads its size class on math and code, trails on knowledge benchmarks. Best: MATH-500 at 98.2, the top score in webAI’s comparison. Worst: GPQA Diamond at 70.2, 11.5 points behind Qwen3.5-9B. HLE is 12.6 (verbose variant). What is TwIL-8B? TwIL-8B is a dense decoder-only reasoning model from webAI. It has 40 layers, hidden size 4096, and 32 attention heads with 8 KV heads . Input and output are English text only. The model writes a <think> block before each answer. It ships in 2 variants with the same architecture and tokenizer. Balanced is the default and produces shorter reasoning traces. Verbose reasons longer and targets hard contest-style problems. TwIL-8B extends webAI’s TwIL family. The first members were 1.7B and 3B formal-logic models released in August 2026. How was TwIL-8B trained? webAI used 3 post-training stages : Full-parameter SFT on reasoning traces for math, STEM and instruction following. GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning on math, code, STEM and instruction prompts. This produces the verbose variant. Length-aware RL with a reward that favors shorter traces against per-domain length references. This produces the balanced variant. Training pools were decontaminated with 13-gram matching against AIME, HMMT, MATH-500, GPQA and other evals. How does TwIL-8B perform on benchmarks? All TwIL-8B scores are self-reported, high-effort pass@1 with thinking enabled. Scores marked † were measured on the verbose variant only. Math : TwIL-8B scores 98.2 on MATH-500. Qwen3.5-9B lists 96.6 on a third-party leaderboard . Gemma 4 31B scored 87.9 in Red Hat’s lighteval run . On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B posts 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On AIME 2026 it scores 88.3, behind Qwen3.5-9B at 92.5 and Gemma 4 31B at 89.2 . Code : LiveCodeBench† is 81.6, against 65.6 for Qwen3.5-9B and 80.0 for Gemma 4 31B. webAI notes its LiveCodeBench version was not recorded. Competitor scores are v6. Instruction following : IFBench† is 74.4, 9.9 points above Qwen3.5-9B at 64.5. IFEval is level, at 91.8 vs 91.5. Knowledge : This is the weak spot. GPQA Diamond is 70.2, against 81.7 for Qwen3.5-9B and 84.3 for Gemma 4 31B. MMLU-Pro† is 76.5 vs 82.5 for Qwen3.5-9B. Across 13 shared benchmarks, TwIL-8B goes 7-6 against Qwen3.5-9B. Against Gemma 4 31B, about 3.5x its size, it goes 3-11. Does TwIL-8B use fewer reasoning tokens? Yes, against its closest open peer. On AIME 2026, TwIL-8B averages about 19.5k output tokens per problem. Qwen3.5-9B uses 31.2k, so TwIL-8B uses 38% fewer. It scores 4.2 points lower. On HMMT Feb 2026 the gap is 32.9k vs 40.6k, or 19% fewer. Frontier models remain far leaner. webAI cites about 5k tokens per AIME 2026 problem for GPT-5.5. webAI states that harnesses and tokenizers differ, so treat this as directional. articles.title: Giving a macOS App Group Its Own Dock Icon: Design Lessons From Cybokron Dock Groups
articles.content: A group of applications is easy to describe and surprisingly awkward to represent in a desktop interface. A developer might need an editor, a terminal, and a browser together, yet the Dock presents them as separate applications. Cybokron Dock Groups treats that collection as a named unit: something that can have its own icon, open its members, or hide them together. The interesting engineering problem is not the list of apps. It is making the group fit macOS without pretending it is a separate desktop session. Disclosure: I am Ercan Atay, the developer of Cybokron Dock Groups, and have a direct interest in the project. This article was prepared with AI drafting assistance based on the project's public documentation. It is a developer's technical explanation, not an independent product review. A group is not a saved session. Consider a hypothetical Development group containing an editor, a terminal, a browser, and a documentation website. Opening that group should have a narrow, predictable meaning. It should launch applications that are closed, bring running applications forward, and open the website in the default browser. It should not imply that a terminal command will resume, that a browser tab will return to a specific state, or that every window will move to a particular display. Those are different problems. Keeping that boundary explicit avoids promising a workspace-restoration system when the underlying object is a collection of launch targets. The same distinction matters for ending work. Hide All hides only running member applications; it does not launch closed ones. Close All asks the group's running applications to quit normally. Force quit is a separate action, available through Command-click. It is not interchangeable with hiding, and it can discard unsaved work. That gives the group a small vocabulary rather than a vague “switch workspace” command. The vocabulary is easier to explain because each action has a separate consequence. Why a Dock icon becomes an app bundle. A group can live in a menu-bar menu, but a persistent Dock entry needs something macOS can recognize. Cybokron's standalone mode creates a small application bundle for each group. The bundle lives under the user's Application Support directory. It contains a copy of the project's executable, its own Info.plist, a group-specific bundle identifier, a group-config.json resource, and the group's icon. The executable runs in an agent role rather than creating another full menu-bar instance. This is not just an alias to a list. The group has an application identity that can be registered with LaunchServices. Clicking its Dock icon toggles the popup; Option-click opens the group's members. The standalone agent can do this even when the main menu-bar app is not running. There is a cost to that independence. A changed group needs its generated bundle updated, and a running agent needs to reload its configuration. A renamed group also needs its bundle path and Dock entry updated. The project repository documents these mechanics, including ad hoc signing and verification of the generated agents. These generated bundles should not be confused with the Developer ID-signed main application. Dock integration has observable side effects. Adding a generated application to the Dock means changing persistent Dock entries. In this implementation, the Dock briefly restarts to display the change. That is a real side effect, not something a utility should conceal behind a claim of seamlessness. The project keeps backups of the Dock's application list before writing it and retains the newest six. If it cannot read the existing list, it does not rewrite the Dock or disable groups on that basis. This is an important failure boundary: inability to understand an existing user configuration should not become permission to replace it. The broader lesson is to design the failure path alongside the feature. A Dock icon is convenient, but preserving the user's existing Dock is…

articles.title: Stop Trusting Notification URLs
articles.content: TL;DR: Every bid response a DSP sends carries URLs that anyone who has seen the response can call: impression, click, win, billing. Most DSPs count whatever comes in, which is where discrepancy reports come from. We treated a notification URL like a cheque: valid only if we issued it, for that bid, and it hasn’t been cashed. The bidder mints hashes and a spend reservation at bid time; every callback is checked against them, duplicates and replays are rejected, and unclaimed reservations expire after 45 minutes. Result: about 6% of callbacks rejected as unverifiable, and reported impressions within 1% of the exchanges’ figures. Every bid response a DSP sends contains a set of URLs: call this one when the ad is shown, this one when it is clicked, this one when the auction is won, this one when it is billed. The exchange, the publisher’s page, and anyone else who has seen the response can call them. Most DSPs count whatever comes in. That is the quiet reason discrepancy reports exist. Not fraud, usually, though fraud rides along happily. Mostly it is duplicate calls, replayed calls, calls from cached responses that never rendered, and callbacks for auctions the DSP did not win. Every one of them becomes an impression in a report, a dollar in an invoice, and an argument with an advertiser. When I built the bidder for Mobinner’s DSP, I treated a notification URL the way a bank treats a cheque: it is only good if we issued it, for that amount, and it has not been cashed already. Mint at bid time, verify at callback. The mechanism is simple. When a bidder node decides to bid, it does three things before it responds. It reserves the bid amount against the campaign budget in a shared store, so that parallel nodes cannot spend the same dollar twice. It generates a set of hashes, one for the conversion and one for each tracking event, and stores them alongside the reservation. And it embeds those hashes in the notification URLs it returns. When a callback arrives, the handler does not count it. It looks up the hashes for that bid and compares. If they match, the event is written to reporting, the hash is cleared so the same event cannot be counted twice, and the spend is committed. If they do not match, or there is no reservation, the call is rejected, and nothing is recorded. If no callback ever arrives, the reservation expires after 45 minutes, and a cleaner service returns the budget to the campaign; conversion hashes live 48 hours, because conversions arrive late. The result is that a notification URL has no value to anyone except the winner of the bid it was issued for, and that nothing reaches a report unless it was bid for, won, and seen once. What it costs. A write to the shared store on every bid, and a read on every callback. That is not free at scale, and it is the reason some DSPs skip it: the bid path is where milliseconds matter, and a store round trip is a visible cost. We judged it worth paying, because the alternative is reconciling discrepancies by hand every month, which costs more and never ends. In a typical month, we rejected roughly 6% of incoming callbacks as unverifiable, and our reported impressions came within 1% of the exchanges’ own figures. Why this matters more now. Three things have changed since this design was new. Supply-path optimisation means a DSP sees the same impression through several paths, and duplicate callbacks are a feature of the plumbing, not a bug. Server-side rendering and prefetching mean more responses are generated than are ever shown. And the gap between a bid and its billing notice is where most of the money in programmatic goes missing. A DSP that counts callbacks on trust is making a promise to advertisers it cannot keep. The fix is not a fraud vendor bolted on afterwards; it is refusing, at the point of counting, to count anything you did not issue. articles.content: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak today shared an Apple TV video that offers a look at how "Resident Evil" director Zach Cregger uses an iPhone during filmmaking. Cregger said he uses his iPhone and the Cadrage app to plan out filming sequences ahead of time. He decides what shots to take, what lenses to use for each shot, and what's in each frame. He then prints out the images so the crew knows exactly what to do. According to Cregger, he used this process for "Weapons" and "Barbarian," two movies that he wrote and directed. He said every scene in those films was planned with photos in advance. articles.title: Netflix Launches First AI-Branded Content Recommendations Feature on TVs
articles.content: Netflix is testing its first consumer-facing feature explicitly branded as AI-powered. Called "AI Discover," the feature generates personalized TV and movie recommendations in real time based on viewing history, preferences, trending content and selectable themes like "Something Light" or "Quick Watches." Variety reports: The streamer will begin rolling out AI Discover in the U.S. to customers who use Netflix in English on supported smart TVs. If you have access to it, you will see a "Discover" tab with a red gem-shaped icon and a "New" label in the top navigation bar on your TV. The company plans to expand the feature to more regions and customers in the coming weeks. Netflix has long used machine-learning and AI technologies to personalize content recommendations, but AI Discover is the first user-facing application that the company is branding as powered by artificial intelligence. The hope is that the AI-recommended titles will be another tool to drive up Netflix's total watch time among viewers, especially in the U.S. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed
articles.content: During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: the project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using. This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today. In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down ten such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Apple turns iCloud into spy cloud, will start looking at public share links
articles.content: If you share content using public iCloud links, Apple could soon be looking over your shoulder and checking for "harmful content." The iBiz announced plans to moderate publicly accessible iCloud share links in version 27.3 of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS on a support page published on Tuesday. To clarify, this applies only to iCloud content shared via links created to be accessible to anyone, as opposed to content shared directly with other people. “Items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content,” Apple explained on the new help page without bothering to define what harmful content means. Based on the wording, it appears those checks will apply to all iCloud items shared using "Anyone with the Link," which Apple says it can also access. The company hasn't explained how the checks will work. The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection , Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for supported iCloud data, remains enabled for the account. “If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time,” the help page continues, adding that the iMaker may also block or disable accounts associated with harmful content. The company also said it reserves the right to involve law enforcement when necessary, suggesting that its undefined "harmful content" category could include child sexual abuse material (CSAM), malware, and other potentially unlawful content. Without a proper definition of what it defines as harmful, however, iCloud users are essentially left at Apple’s mercy: If it chooses to continue to bend the knee to the Trump administration, for example, content deemed objectionable by the standards of political figures could end up wiped out. Apple also hasn't explained whether human moderators, automated systems, or both will be responsible for identifying and removing so-called harmful content, or whether any decisions will be left to AI, which can easily be fooled into making a bad moderation call. The scanning of such content, as mentioned above, begins with version 27.3 of Apple’s various OSes, which were released to developers in beta on Tuesday, with a general release expected in December. Apple didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

articles.title: Apple is Putting Employees on an AI Budget
articles.content: Apple is curtailing employee AI use to cut costs, reports Bloomberg . In October, Apple limited some engineers to $200 per day for AI spending, down from $300. More cuts could be coming, with daily allowances for some engineers dropping to $100. Many groups outside engineering already have a $100 daily limit, but some teams could have their spending capped at $25. Apple is asking some teams to use less expensive models or switch to on-device AI. Employees who need a bigger budget will be able to ask executives for an increase. Engineers at Apple have the largest budgets because using AI for coding can consume a large number of tokens. Apple lets employees use Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and other models. Some Apple employees told Bloomberg that few were using their full $300 daily limit, so the savings may be small. Apple has also hired outside productivity consultants for some divisions. Combined with the AI cost cuts, the reviews have fueled worries about possible restructuring. Apple CEO John Ternus took over on September 1, and he reportedly wants to reduce corporate hierarchy and bloat to accomplish more with fewer people. This article, " Apple is Putting Employees on an AI Budget " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: We Stopped Feeding LLMs Raw HTML: Cutting Agent Scraping Costs by 74% Across 10,000 Targets
articles.content: Every AI agent demo looks the same. You pass a URL to a scraper, hand the returned text to a model, and get clean JSON back. It works beautifully — right up until you point it at the real internet. We were building an autonomous agent to track enterprise GPU availability: H100, H200, and Blackwell server rentals across cloud providers, wholesale distributor dashboards, and secondary marketplace brokers. The goal was simple. Watch thousands of supply points, detect availability and price shifts, and flag them before competitors noticed. It collapsed in four days. Not because the model was weak, but because the plumbing underneath it was naive. Three things broke at once. Failure One: The Anti-Bot Perimeter Roughly 78% of our target portals sat behind Cloudflare Turnstile, DataDome, or Akamai. Headless Chromium containers looped on challenges until the concurrency pool drained into a wall of HTTP 403s. The agent wasn't slow. It was locked out. Failure Two: The Context Explosion Raw HTML dumps burned between 12,000 and 18,000 tokens per page. We were paying a model to read cookie consent banners, minified JavaScript, inline SVG sprites, and tracking pixel URLs — then wondering why it occasionally hallucinated prices that weren't on the page. Failure Three: The Proxy Bill Premium residential bandwidth runs $8 to $15 per gigabyte. Downloading hero images, web fonts, and analytics beacons across 10,000 hourly targets meant infrastructure cost more than the arbitrage margin we were chasing. A system that is profitable on paper and cash-negative in practice is not a product. It is an expensive hobby. The lesson that reshaped the whole design: an agent cannot reason over data it cannot reach, and it cannot stay cheap if every fetch is a paid browser session. The Fix: Route by cost, not by habit. Our original pipeline sent every request through a rotating proxy and a full headless render. That is paying premium prices to read public pages. We replaced it with three tiers of escalation. The rule: escalate only when the previous tier actually fails. Tier 0 — Direct HTTP/2 (free). An async request with browser-accurate TLS fingerprints. If the response is a 200 with no mitigation signatures, we take the payload and move on. Documentation endpoints, status feeds, older portals, sitemaps, and RSS all die here, at zero marginal cost. Tier 1 — Bright Data Web Unlocker (~$0.0015/request). Triggered by a 403, a 429, or mitigation headers such as cf-ray or datadome-challenge. It handles fingerprint emulation, CAPTCHA solving, and IP rotation, which means we stopped maintaining our own cookie jars and proxy reputation lists — an entire class of maintenance work disappeared. Tier 2 — Bright Data Scraping Browser. Only about 14% of targets genuinely need client-side rendering: React and Vue dashboards that hydrate pricing tables over WebSockets after load. Instead of running Chromium locally, we connect to a cloud browser over CDP and block images, CSS, and fonts at the network interception layer before a single byte is downloaded. That single decision — connect to a remote browser instead of spawning a local one — cut memory per worker from 640 MB to 38 MB, and it took fingerprint-based honeypots out of the equation entirely. Stop feeding models the whole DOM. A 2.4 MB e-commerce page usually contains under 4 KB of useful data. We built a deterministic pre-processor with two stages. Stage 1: JSON-LD harvester. Retailers expose schema.org product and price data for Google, so we read that first. About 320 tokens, zero LLM calls, no hallucination surface. If a valid schema exists, the model never runs at all. Stage 2: density pruning. If no schema exists, we strip script, style, svg, iframe, nav, and footer; score nodes by text-to-tag ratio; drop low-density containers such as menus and cookie banners; and emit the remainder as Markdown tables. The model receives structure, not noise. That is the difference between an extraction agent and an…

articles.title: VMware releases vSphere Express for virtualization on up to 128 cores
articles.content: After alienating many long-time small- to medium-sized business (SMB) customers, Broadcom’s VMware is trying to appeal to its smaller customers. Today, the virtualization company announced vSphere Express, a lower-end virtualization offering for organizations that require “cost-effective essential virtualization.” vSphere Express comes after many customers reported that VMware was pushing them to VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), the flagship private cloud bundle that has many features SMBs don’t need and is expensive. Some SMB users have reported that VMware sales representatives previously told them that vSphere Standard, VMware's prior entry-level virtualization offering, wasn’t available anymore. articles.title: Over half of readers say T-Mobile has lost its Un-Carrier edge
articles.content: The big three US carriers now form a sort of monolith in the minds of customers, but there was a time when they really managed to differentiate themselves, largely thanks to their advertising. T-Mobile’s involved its hard-to-ignore magenta shade and its even harder-to-ignore CEO John Legere, who tirelessly promoted the “un-carrier.” But Legere hasn’t been at the helm since 2020 and T-Mobile has undone a lot of the policies he put in place. So we asked our readers: Is T-Mobile still worth it in 2026? Out of 1,423 of you who responded, 53% said no, not really.

articles.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
articles.content: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company's gaming segment cratered. AMD CFO Jean Hu said, "We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our Data Center segment." AMD says its Q4 revenue projections are up another 27 percent from this quarter's results. As reported by Tom's Hardware , Intel's Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel's revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD's business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs . Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year. Read full article Comments

articles.title: ChatGPT finally adds the image tool the internet has been waiting for
articles.content: TL;DR ChatGPT is getting animated GIF generation, letting users turn text prompts and uploaded photos into short animations. Users will be able to adjust playback speed from 0.5x to 2x and edit individual frames. OpenAI’s Images 2.6 update is rolling out to ChatGPT and Codex across web, desktop, and mobile, with faster image generation also included. Sometimes, GIFs can say what a thousand words can’t. A quick peek at my group chats would prove just that — there’s no shortage of ways to communicate without actually typing a word. I’ve normally relied on repositories like Giphy and Tenor for my GIF needs, though this popular AI tool might soon give me, and you, a way to give GIFs a more personal touch. The tool I’m talking about is ChatGPT , and in addition to image generation, it will now also let you generate and edit GIFS, as highlighted by The Verge .

articles.title: Apple TV's '12 Days of Snoopy' Special Arrives November 13
articles.content: Apple today shared a trailer for a new Snoopy special that's airing on Friday, November 13. "Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy" features Snoopy working to get off Santa's naughty list ahead of Christmas. In the latest special of the acclaimed "Snoopy Presents" banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa's naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he's not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts. The special has original music from John Legend, Kamasi Washington featuring Leon Bridges, and Laufey. Apple TV has exclusive rights to Peanuts content, including the classic library and original shows and specials. Snoopy content available on ‌Apple TV‌ includes "Snoopy in Space," "The Snoopy Show," "It's the Small Things, Charlie Brown," "Lucy's School," and more. Apple is offering free streaming of "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving" on November 14 and 15, and "A Charlie Brown Christmas" on December 12 and 13. An ‌Apple TV‌ subscription is not required to watch the classic Charlie Brown specials on those days. Apple's streaming television service is priced at $14.99 per month and available in more than 100 countries and regions. articles.title: Bose’s QuietComfort Headphones are more than half off
articles.content: It’s not often that some of the best noise-canceling headphones you can buy are over half off. But right now, the first-gen Bose QuietComfort Headphones are on sale for $169.99 ($190 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , and Bose , matching its best price to date. The newer, second-generation version that launched in August is also down to $199 ($160 off) in multiple colors at Amazon , Best Buy , and directly from Bose , which is just $20 shy of the all-time low price. They also support multipoint Bluetooth connectivity, so you can connect to two devices simultaneously, and they feature a lightweight, foldable design that makes them easy to pack. The second-generation QuietComfort Headphones build on that foundation with a few worthwhile upgrades for $30 more. articles.title: Ricursive AI Releases Ripple-65B Preview: A 65B Dense Open-Weight Model Scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1
articles.content: Ricursive Intelligence just released Ripple-65B Preview . Ripple-65B Preview is a 65B dense open-weight model from Ricursive, pretrained from scratch for agentic coding. It is a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind Ricursive’s AI chip design platform. The main claim: 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 , the top self-reported score among US open-weight models. Every MoE rival it beats on that test carries 501B to 975B total parameters. TL;DR Size: 65B dense (65B active), pretrained on 12T tokens, up to 1M context. Runs on: BF16 on datacenter GPUs (250 tok/s on 2x B200). Experimental NVFP4 build targets NVIDIA DGX Spark. Performance: Frontier-level agentic coding for its size; trails larger MoE models on knowledge and science coding. Best: Terminal-Bench 2.1, 80.5 (self-reported). Worst: SciCode, 39.4, lowest of the 5 models in Ricursive’s own table. What is Ripple-65B Preview? The release includes 3 checkpoints : an instruction-tuned BF16 model, an NVFP4 version , and a BF16 base model . All ship under Apache 2.0. Pretraining used a text-only corpus, mostly English and code, at 8K sequence length. Ricursive team states that the full R&D cost was $32M . That figure covers ladder experiments, data mixing, evals, synthetic data and the final runs. Ricursive team estimates that it is one-tenth the cost of the prior open-weight agentic coding leader. How does the architecture work? Ricursive chose a dense Transformer over Mixture-of-Experts to reduce infrastructure complexity. Training held 40% MFU with simple sharding, no custom kernels and no quantization. The model is thin and deep: a d_model of 5120 across 80 layers. It moves from Olmo 3’s Llama-like layout to a Gemma 3N-like design for stability. Key choices: Overprovisioned attention heads for reasoning, offset by more sliding-window layers and smaller windows. Gated attention , global NoPE and value residuals . FFN activation clipping , a technique also used in gpt-oss . Ricursive team built the recipe through laddering experiments starting from Olmo 3’s ladder . It rejected changes that failed to hold at 4B scale, such as 2-stream mHC. The technical post reports a 16x code compute-efficiency gain at 4B scale. How was it post-trained? Post-training ran midtraining, long context, SFT, long-context SFT and mixed RL. Long-context stages trained at 2M sequence length. Ricursive bought no post-training data and built its own synthetic pipelines. The RL recipe combines truncated importance sampling , score centering and a linear length penalty . Ripple hit 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 1.4M rollouts. Ricursive puts that at roughly 70x fewer than Beam, which reported over 100M rollouts . How does Ripple-65B compare on benchmarks? Ricursive team ran missing evals in-house using OpenCode, and Terminus 2 for SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard and DeepSWE 1.1. Scores below are Ricursive’s presented data. Terminal-Bench 2.1: 80.5, vs Beam 80.1 , Muse Spark Open 76.4 , Inkling 63.8 , Nemotron 3 Ultra 56.4 . SWE-bench Pro v2.0 Hard: 79.1, the top score in Ricursive’s table. SWE-bench Verified: 76.5, below Beam and Inkling. Math: 98.3 on AIME 2025 and 90.5 on HMMT Feb 2026. Weak spots: SciCode 39.4, DeepSWE 1.1 44.3, MCP Atlas 71.67, GPQA Diamond 85.2. Ricursive team also reran Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the official Terminus 2 harness at 128K. Most rivals dropped there; Beam fell to 70.8. Muse Spark Open rose to 78.7, still below Ripple’s 80.5. articles.title: Waymo Cuts Ties With Uber, Will Serve Riders Directly
articles.content: Waymo plans to end its exclusive Uber robotaxi partnership in Austin and Atlanta in January 2028 and let customers hail its vehicles directly through the Waymo app. In an interview on The Circuit, Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana called the current Uber experience a "crapshoot" because riders aren't guaranteed a Waymo. Bloomberg reports: "In the early days, we would partner because we didn't have the scale, and in that partnering, it was a little bit of a crapshoot. Will I get a Waymo? Will I not get a Waymo?," Mawakana said in a wide-ranging interview on The Circuit with Emily Chang. She cited customers' growing demand for a consistent offering from a single app, especially from riders from San Francisco or other markets, where Waymo offers the self-driving service via its own consumer app that competes with Uber. "It's important for us to have that relationship with the rider. We've gotten that feedback from the riders in those markets," Mawakana said. "And at the same time, learning and partnering with Uber has been a really important part of our journey," she added. [...] The comments reflect Waymo's evolving relationship with the ride-hailing giant as the Alphabet unit trials different pathways to commercialize its capital-intensive autonomous technology. Waymo has leaned on partners like Uber and Lyft, as well as fleet management companies, to help operate its roughly 4,000 vehicles across the US. The company currently does more than 500,000 trips per week in 14 cities. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
