articles.title: Bare metal boom: On-prem server sales for HPC and AI up 20% this year
articles.content: On-premises high-performance compute (HPC) is still in demand, according to Hyperion Research, which estimates the market is expanding at almost 20 percent year-on-year, often driven by requirements for AI processing. What Hyperion calls the "on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science" server market showed significant growth in the first half of 2026, with revenues hitting $16.5 billion, up 19.9 percent. However, the analyst says unit shipments over the same period grew only 4.4 percent, meaning that systems are carrying a higher price tag due to greater use of costly components such as GPUs and other accelerators, not to mention the effects of higher memory costs, which have tripled or quadrupled since last year. Its tracking of the HPC market is based on multiple surveys conducted of both buyers and suppliers, the firm says. The latest data shows a major change in the overall HPC market growth, heavily driven by a combination of the use of AI, large language models (LLMs), and purchases of large GPU/accelerator-based systems. This trend was noted a couple of years ago, with Omdia reporting in 2024 that revenue growth from server sales was racing ahead of actual units shipped, as customers prioritized investment in highly configured server clusters for AI . Much of that spending was by hyperscalers and cloud providers, seeking to profit from selling AI services to enterprise customers, but Hyperion’s figures focus on on-prem shipments, showing that many enterprises prefer to do their processing in-house. According to Hyperion, Dell has now surpassed HPE as the biggest HPC vendor, with server revenues of $4.2 billion for the first half of 2026. HPE, which picked up supercomputing specialist Cray for $1.3 billion in 2019, had long been pack leader in the global HPC arena in terms of market share and revenue. The figures put Dell on a 24 percent share, while HPE is not far behind on 21 percent. Lenovo and China-based Sugon trail behind at 4 percent share each, while 45 percent of the market is just labelled as "others" by Hyperion. This includes names such as Bull, which re-emerged from the shadows of Atos this year, plus Supermicro, Penguin Computing, and NEC. The HPC infrastructure market is inherently cyclical. HPE recognized significant revenue in 2025 with sales of multiple exascale-class leadership machines, but procurement of that scale is intermittent and doesn't necessarily come along every year, Hyperion notes. "Organizations and institutions are continuing to invest in their advanced computing infrastructure due to both replacing aging machines and the desire to adopt AI into their workflows to support their businesses and missions," said Hyperion Research CEO Earl Joseph. "The growth reflects both a nominal increase in units being purchased and significant increases in system prices." HPC systems are considered the backbone for many AI and AI-related applications, which has driven the overall HPC market to a new growth level, Joseph added. ®

Furthermore, Gibson says that the NT$37.8 billion capital expenditure is allocated to NOR and NAND Flash, leaving none for ROM as the company shifts its manufacturing capacity to supply AI needs — Taipei Times corroborated the report, stating, "At the same time, Macronix is gradually phasing out of ROM production, Wu said. It also reports that Macronix’s capital expenditure is split into two phases, the NT$ 22 billion for expanding manufacturing capacity, followed by an additional NT$15.8 billion for NAND flash used in eMMCs and 3D NAND. Gibson expects that Nintendo’s digital margins will grow through more Game-Key Cards or digital-only sales, but as Macronix isn’t the only source of ROM chips, “physical cards will likely carry on for some time.” Gibson further reports that digital margins have been slowly rising, with numbers fluctuating depending on the quarter due to major physical game launches. 3/4 My view: Macronix isn't Nintendo's only game memory card maker, so physical cards will likely carry on for some time. But at the margin, digital will grow, through more Game-Key Cards (which hold a download key, not the game) and digital-only sales. November 4, 2026 ROHM group companies ROHM Semiconductor and LAPIS Semiconductor still supply ROM chips to Nintendo, so it’s unlikely that Nintendo will eventually go digital-only in the near future like Sony and Microsoft ’s recent plans. With one less supplier, however, Nintendo may be forced to increase prices on physical games. The biggest loser in all of this (besides the gamers), however, may be fabless chip design company MegaChips. Nintendo doesn’t buy ROM chips from Macronix directly; MegaChips designs the ROM chips according to Nintendo’s needs and, having no manufacturing capacity, outsources it to Macronix. MegaChips’ 2022 company report states that Nintendo accounted for 87.8% of its sales, while Macronix accounted for 67.8% of its outsourced manufacturing purchases. The report even states that if Macronix could manufacture ROM chips, “MegaChips’ operating results may be impacted.” The 2022 document further says that there was no sign that the risk would become apparent; however, the risk just became very real, and we’re not aware of MegaChips’ contingency plan to deal with this situation. However, Macronix and MegaChips have likely talked amongst themselves about Macronix’s plans to stop ROM chip manufacturing, and have given MegaChips some time to find another manufacturer before Macronix shuts…

articles.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
articles.content: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago. While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level. Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before. What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto. So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election. There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process. The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump. With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations. Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout. Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data…

The series also explores the personal relationships and defining moments that shaped the man behind the legendary boxing career. Why you should watch it: Muhammad Ali's story is fascinating, making this a great watch for sports fans and anyone who enjoys a compelling real-life documentary. Beyond his achievements in the boxing ring, the series offers a closer look at the man behind the famous name and the experiences that shaped his remarkable life. It's also a great opportunity to revisit one of the most memorable periods in sporting history. Watch "The Greatest" on Prime Video now ‘Stick’ (season 2 premiere) (Apple TV) Genre: Sports comedy series What it's about: Teenage golf prodigy Santi (Peter Dager) takes the next step towards professional golf, discovering that talent comes with plenty of pressure. Owen Wilson brings plenty of charm to the series, while its golf setting gives the story a fun backdrop for some genuinely heartwarming character moments. There's plenty here to enjoy even if you're not particularly interested in golf, thanks to its focus on relationships, second chances and finding your feet. articles.title: Japanese Bank to Stop Allowing ATM Cards, PCs For Account Access
articles.content: Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group plans to launch Emut Bank in early 2027 as the first digital bank affiliated with a major Japanese financial institution to eliminate ATM cards, "instead having customers confirm identities using the bank's smartphone app for additional security amid a rising tide of cyberattacks," reports Nikkei Asia Review. The smartphone app will also be the only way to manage deposits, with no PC-based banking. From the report: Security has become a greater concern recently. As artificial intelligence advances, Japan has seen a surge in cyberattacks targeting companies, as well as a rise in phishing attacks aimed at stealing personal information, often targeting bank accounts. The technology being used by Emut was developed by Seven Bank, the consumer finance unit of Seven & i Holdings, operator of 7-Eleven convenience stores. Emut customers will be able to withdraw money from Seven Bank's roughly 28,000 ATMs. The network is expected to gradually expand to cover the 16,000 or so ATMs at FamilyMart convenience stores. Although MUFG Bank ATMs will not be accessible, MUFG will consider changing this in the future. Scrapping cash cards represents a shift in what has for decades been consumers' main method of withdrawing money. The former Sumitomo Bank -- a predecessor of Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. -- is believed to have been Japan's first bank to implement cash cards, in 1969. The step away from cash cards by MUFG, Japan's largest financial institution, is likely to spur other banks to follow suit. [...] Eschewing cash cards will reduce Emut's costs, which will let it offer interest rates on deposits that are expected to be higher than MUFG Bank's usual 0.5%, depending on the terms. Interest can be paid out daily, rather than twice a year -- a first for a Japanese bank. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: “Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying”: Anthropic’s fix puts Claude in the identity business
articles.content: Anthropic is now letting businesses automatically connect employees to approved Claude plugins, saving staff from having to sign in to and authorize each service individually. The feature also allows Claude to verify users’ organizational membership directly, making it easier for companies to manage access to workplace applications. The feature builds on the Enterprise-Managed Authorization ( EMA ) extension to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which debuted back in June. As The New Stack reported at the time , this ushered in a way for companies to manage MCP connections centrally through their existing identity providers, with Okta becoming the first to support it. Anthropic also announced support for the extension in Claude, Claude Code and Cowork on the same day, and published implementation guidance for developers building compatible MCP servers. In its original guise, the approach relied on the company’s identity provider being compatible with EMA. Okta was the first to support the extension, and adoption among other providers remains limited, meaning many organizations have still had to authorize connections individually. “Claude itself can issue the signed identity assertions that participating MCP services use to recognize employees.” On the ClaudeDevs X account on Tuesday, Anthropic introduced another option : Claude itself can issue the signed identity assertions that participating MCP services use to recognize employees. This effectively means businesses can enable automatic connections without requiring their identity provider to support the extension. “If you’re building plugins for Claude, add support so users get started faster and stay connected without re-authorizing,” the company writes. The new Claude authorization feature is available in beta now, for Team and Enterprise customers. Claude takes over the identity check Taking to X on Tuesday, Boris Cherny , head of applications at Anthropic, points to the frustration of employees having to repeatedly authenticate workplace applications. “Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying.” “Signing in to your company’s plugins one by one is annoying, so we let Claude auto-connect to them now,” Cherny writes . Signing in to your company's plugins one by one is annoying, so we let Claude auto-connect to them now. Team and Enterprise admins can set them up, and teammates are connected automatically the first time they use the plugins. https://t.co/w2oxw0bKOZ — Boris Cherny (@bcherny) November 3, 2026 Administrators can choose which supported services to enable, and which employee roles should receive access. For example, a company might be comfortable giving all employees access to a general-purpose productivity tool, while restricting access to more sensitive systems, such as company databases, to specific roles because of the risks associated with exposing confidential information or making unauthorized changes. When an eligible user opens a plugin, Claude sends a signed assertion identifying them as a member of the organization. The receiving service checks that assertion before providing an access token. The process also handles subsequent connections automatically, so users don’t have to repeatedly authorize the same service when tokens expire. The initial rollout spans a broad array of more than a dozen services, including Amplitude, Apollo.io, Atlassian, Datadog, Dropbox, Figma, Granola, HubSpot, Linear, Mixpanel, Notion, PagerDuty, Semrush, and Supabase. 14 services have signed up to Claude’s auto-connect plugins at launch. In a November 3 blog post , Supabase explained that customers can now use Claude to authenticate employees accessing its MCP server, even if their identity provider lacks EMA support. articles.title: T-Mobile launches $90 5 Gbps fiber internet plan
articles.content: Just over a year ago, T-Mobile launched its home fiber internet service in the United States, buoyed by its acquisition of Lumos. At the time, T-Mobile’s fiber service reached half a million customers across the country, with speeds of up to 2 Gbps. This week, T-Mobile introduced a new 5 Gbps tier for customers who crave even more speed. The 5 Gbps tier is priced at $90 per month and comes with a 10-year price guarantee. Given how often legacy cable internet providers would raise prices, forcing customers to jump through hoops to keep the status quo, a 10-year price lock could be very appealing to a large segment of the population. But as with most things, there is some fine print to the offer, which reads, “Taxes & fees, voluntary equipment or speed upgrades, select limited-time promotions, per-use charges, third-party services, and network management practices aren’t included.” To get the $90/month price, you’ll also need to set up AutoPay with T-Mobile. However, to further sweeten the deal, customers will also receive a mesh Wi-Fi extender that broadens the coverage of the included Fiber gateway. For new customers, T-Mobile is also offering two months of free service (via bill credits) and a $300 virtual prepaid debit card. T-Mobile’s pricing for the 5 Gbps plan is an aggressive deal in the home fiber market. For example, GFiber (Google) costs $100/month for 3 Gbps speeds, while the company’s 8 Gbps tier is $150/month. (Image credit: T-Mobile) T-Mobile’s new 5 Gbps plan joins the existing 2 Gbps ($70/month), 1 Gbps ($60/month), and 300 Mbps ($45/month) plans. All of the plans feature symmetrical upload/download speeds, which is a big upgrade for anyone coming from a traditional cable internet provider. For people who don’t have access to T-Mobile’s growing fiber footprint in the U.S., the company also offers its unlimited 5G Home Internet service , with prices starting at $50/month.
articles.author: Brandon Hill

articles.title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
articles.content: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. How eligible actions are reviewed Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service. An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions. The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant…

articles.title: “The team stopped arguing — and that’s bad news”: the anatomy of a socio-technical conflict
articles.content: If the product and technical teams have suddenly stopped arguing, don’t be too quick to celebrate. Perhaps they have genuinely learnt to reach agreements, but there is another possibility: the arguments have simply lost their meaning. I’ve seen the latter scenario play out several times. At first, the engineers raise concerns, arguing about technical debt, architecture or deadlines; then they realise that this doesn’t change the outcome, and gradually fall silent. From the outside, things even seem to improve: fewer arguments, faster planning, easier decision-making. But the problem is that, along with the conflict, important feedback may disappear from the system. Let’s take a closer look at this particular scenario. What is conflict? In everyday terms, “conflict” is usually associated with a dispute, confrontation or even a crisis in relations. We are accustomed to thinking of it as an anomaly to be avoided, but in any complex system where different parties are working towards a common goal, conflict is a natural reaction to the fact that participants view that common goal from different perspectives. I find Thomas Schelling’s perspective in The Strategy of Conflict particularly relevant here. He deals with situations where the parties are neither pure allies nor pure adversaries: some of their interests coincide, others do not, but they are nonetheless dependent on one another to achieve their own goals. The interaction between product and technical teams is very similar to this. If we apply this logic to product development, I can see at least three areas where interests regularly diverge: Speed vs. stability. It’s important for the business to get results sooner, whilst engineers need to ensure the next change doesn’t end up costing three times as much. This, in particular, is the classic conflict surrounding technical debt, the nature of which I wrote about in my previous article, Technical Debt: Manage It, Don’t Conquer It . Tactics vs. strategy. Sometimes a hypothesis really does need to be tested within a week, even though a technically sound solution would take a month. Boundaries of autonomy. Who decides exactly what we are building, and who decides how it will be implemented. These contradictions do not in themselves mean that something is wrong with the company. On the contrary, they are entirely natural, and in practice these three contradictions rarely exist in isolation. Let’s say a product needs to be launched with new functionality in two weeks. First, we argue about speed and stability: can we afford to make a technical compromise to meet the deadline? Then we discuss tactics and strategy: is this really a temporary solution to test a hypothesis, or is it code we’ll have to live with for the next three years? And it can all end in a dispute over autonomy: the product side proposes a specific technical approach because it seems the quickest, whilst the engineers, in response, start arguing not about the risks of the decision, but about who actually has the right to make it. A single product task thus traverses all three dimensions at once. And if there aren’t at least roughly clear rules for each of them, the teams have to negotiate not only the task itself each time, but also how they’re going to reach an agreement in the first place. Where the problem begins Problems arise when the parties view this negotiation as a zero-sum game: if the engineers are given time for refactoring, the business loses a feature; if the business pushes through a release, the engineers lose out. In the short term, this logic even works: you can postpone refactoring, quickly release the required functionality and come back to the problem later. I myself have made such decisions many times, and they were by no means always wrong, but the problem itself begins with the word ‘later’. If one side repeatedly secures a short-term win at the expense of the other, it is not the specific decision that changes, but people’s behaviour in…

articles.title: The Model Proposes. Code Decides.
articles.content: Seven lessons from building and researching customer-facing AI agents that answer with screens Much of what gets written about AI agents is about agents that work for the person using them: coding agents, research agents, office assistants. A customer-facing agent has a harder job. The person on the other side is a stranger, the conversation touches real records and real money, and no colleague is reading along to catch a mistake before it reaches them. We call the version we build an agentic application: a customer-facing agent that answers with screens. After more than a year of building an agent that builds them, these are the key things we’d tell anyone about to put an AI agent in front of their customers, or to buy one. The diagram below is the architecture we think is right. It is our own synthesis of published guidance, research and what we have seen while building. It isn’t a standard. No published study tests this whole architecture, and most of the individual choices in it have no controlled test on real conversations either. Most of the performance numbers we found come from the company selling the product, so we mark those where they appear. Read it from the top. A customer’s message enters through a channel, passes identity and policy checks, and reaches the model. The model sits inside a harness, the code that runs it and enforces the limits around it. From there the model can read (bottom right) or propose an action (bottom left). The left column is where people step in, and the right column is how you measure and improve. At the bottom are your systems of record, which hold the truth. 1. The model proposes, code decides A language model is very good at understanding people and writing back, and it can be talked into things. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) explains why: a model has no inherent distinction between data and instruction. For a customer-facing agent, that means what a customer writes, or what sits on a web page it reads, can change what it does. The pressure doesn’t have to be technical. Reinforce Labs , a vendor that sells testing by attack (red-teaming), attacked 14 live support bots and checked the results against each company’s own published policy. By its count, 28.5% of its 471 attack conversations ended in a policy violation, and unauthorized commitments such as refunds and price matches appeared at 11 of the 14 bots. It says what worked was social, such as emotional pressure and invented urgency, though it gives no success rate per tactic, and its advice is to prepare for an ordinary annoyed customer and not a hacker. The companies aren’t named and nobody has checked the numbers independently. So the model shouldn’t be the gatekeeper. It proposes, and deterministic code, which gives the same result every time, decides. Identity, permissions, money and what the agent is allowed to do are enforced in code, against your records. OWASP , a non-profit security foundation, tells teams to test for exactly this: unauthorized tools, the connections an agent uses to read or change something in your systems, are denied even when the model requests them confidently. In a test by Arize , a vendor that sells monitoring tools, a simulated support agent reading order pages planted with instructions pulled another customer’s record in 28 of 100 runs. Once access was bound in code to the logged-in session, the agent still tried in 20 of 100 runs, and none returned data. That was one model, with no repeat runs. We’d put the check at the moment the action runs, not at an earlier step. One study , on a simulated bank-support benchmark, ran the agent through a fixed workflow and found unauthorized writes no lower than without it, at 4.4% of tasks against 4.3%. The authors think the model can misjudge which step it is on, though they didn’t measure that. Keep the record of the conversation on your server too, not in the visitor’s browser, where it can be faked. Microsoft’s agent framework…

articles.title: The biggest tech story of the midterms might be Democrats’ attorney general wins
articles.content: A blue wave has swept Democrats into control of both the House and Senate , dealing a major blow to Donald Trump in the midterm elections. But beyond the congressional shake-up, a handful of state attorney general races could prove just as consequential for the technology industry. Democrats won five closely watched attorney general races, including a surprise victory in Texas, where Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton to become the state’s first Democratic attorney general since 1994. In Arizona, incumbent Kris Mayes defeated Republican Warren Petersen, while Wisconsin’s Josh Kaul secured a third term. Michigan’s Eli Savit defeated Republican Doug Lloyd to succeed term-limited Democrat Dana Nessel, and Democrat Nicole Cannizzaro won Nevada’s open seat. The results could have huge implications for Big Tech . As federal lawmakers have struggled to rein in the industry, state attorneys general have emerged as some of its most powerful watchdogs, using investigations and lawsuits to force changes to products and practices nationwide. And a change in leadership can bring an abrupt shift in enforcement priorities. “State attorneys general have become the preeminent regulator and regulatory enforcer in the United States over the last 15 or 20 years,” says Stephen Cobb, partner and vice chair of the state attorneys general practice at Foley & Lardner, a Washington, D.C., law firm. “We’ve seen state attorneys general from across the aisle having an increased focus on the technology industries generally,” he adds. Why these races matter for Big Tech Texas, in particular, could signal a major shift. The state’s attorney general’s office has long been among the most influential Republican-led legal operations in the country, regularly helping spearhead multistate lawsuits. Johnson has promised to refocus the office on consumer protection rather than partisan political battles—a change that could reshape the coalitions bringing legal challenges against technology companies. Arizona and Michigan are also important players in tech enforcement. Arizona has been a key participant in multistate actions targeting the industry, while Michigan has been “actively engaged in national consumer protection and technology matters,” says Brandon J. Smith, partner at law firm Holtzman Vogel. “A change in attorney general can mean a significant change in enforcement priorities almost overnight, even without a single change in the underlying law,” Smith says. Attorneys general already have sweeping authority to investigate technology companies, Smith notes. “The technology industry sometimes underestimates just how much authority state attorneys general already possess,” he adds. Even without new AI -specific legislation, state AGs can investigate tech companies using existing consumer protection, unfair and deceptive practices, and antitrust laws. Tech regulation is increasingly bipartisan At first glance, the Democratic sweep might seem like bad news for Big Tech. But the partisan dynamics of tech regulation are more complicated, Smith cautions. Republican attorneys general have generally focused on issues such as alleged censorship and consumer safety, while Democrats have placed greater emphasis on privacy and algorithmic discrimination. But both parties have become increasingly aggressive in their scrutiny of the tech industry, meaning that a Republican victory doesn’t necessarily translate into a friendlier regulatory environment. “Both parties increasingly view big tech as an industry requiring greater scrutiny,” Smith says. “I don’t think technology companies should interpret partisan disagreement as an indication that either side is going to leave them alone.” That bipartisan pressure has been particularly evident in efforts to protect children online. articles.title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
articles.content: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. Post series Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!) The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. What is context engineering? Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “ Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report ” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes. Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing. “As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).” — Anthropic, “ Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents ” (2025.09) Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. This post details the four-layer approach you can apply to manage context efficiently. How to handle tasks that exceed the context window Anthropic has…

articles.title: Is Deep Work Possible Anymore?
articles.content: Agents made software work shallow. Depth now has to be designed. In 2022, I wrote an article about deep work : why it matters for software developers and how to design your time to make it possible in asynchronous, distracting environments. Back then, successful deep work was mainly about managing your interaction with the environment. Keep distraction-free focus time. Work with full concentration. The deep–shallow design of a workday was crucial. The work itself was deep. We just had to protect it. Deep work. Essentialism in asynchronous culture Now it is not enough. In software development, the nature of the work itself changed. Focus on the task was replaced by delegating it to agents and verifying their output. In the past, software development was intrinsically deep (if you were able to find space for it). Today, it has become intrinsically shallow. Intrinsically Shallow A few years ago, a properly designed workday looked something like this. You got a challenging issue: implement a new feature in your system. You found a slot in your calendar. Turned off notifications. Timeboxed the task. Design first, then implementation. All the work is done in high focus on what you read and typed. Now? You read the ticket description. Sometimes you think a little about the problem. But usually you just prompt and delegate the task to the agent. You’re probably working in auto mode, with crafted permissions, so the agent doesn’t bother you with unnecessary questions. The only thing left to do is wait until you can verify. But waiting is boring. It’s hard to sit for a few minutes, still thinking about the problem, while the agent does the work on your behalf. So you switch context to a different problem and fire up another agent. Or read something on the internet. Or reply to a friend. Anything. And your deep work is gone. I don’t think it’s your inability to focus. Delegation and conversation — even with an agent — are intrinsically shallow work. Maybe within one session you can keep your focus on a single topic while tackling a problem with your agent. But in the long run, context switching and distraction become the natural way of working. So the change is not in the design of the day. It’s in the nature of the work. Software is just where agents arrived first. Writers, analysts and designers are next. Surrender by Detachment We can say: it is what it is. The way we work now makes us more productive. We deliver more. There’s no going back to the way we worked in the past. That’s true. But it’s also true that this way of working has side effects. Deep work, I would say, is the way we grow. I genuinely believe it stretches your mind and improves your skills. So the question is whether we can get better without a stable deep work practice. If we lose it, our skills may not only stop improving. They may deteriorate. Addy Osmani writes about cognitive surrender : the more coding you hand to agents, the more you risk losing the very skills needed to supervise them. In the short term, we’re faster and more productive. In the long term, we slowly lose the skills that made us experienced engineers. We become more and more detached from the craft — the same craft we need to verify what agents produce. That’s cognitive surrender. It’s how comprehension debt accumulates. Even if agents can do most of the work — and more of it every year — you still need a skillset to be successful, even if that skillset evolves. Here Be Monsters is a good attempt to map what it looks like. We’ve probably lost deep work as a natural part of our jobs. So where can we still find it? Friction by Design Some people say: “Agents save me time, and I can preserve it for deep work.” It’s a good approach. But it rarely happens on its own. This is the efficiency trap striking again. Improved efficiency doesn’t give us more free time. We just do more work. Our worktime is usually stable; the amount of work is not. The saved time ends up in more delegation and more context…

articles.title: Best RAG Chunking Strategy in 2026? I Benchmarked 5 Methods From New Research
articles.content: RAG chunking strategies compared: complete-evidence recall for five chunkers on the same document, retriever and 120-word context budget. Screenshots from the Chunking Lab (vishalmysore.github.io/advancedRagDemo/chunking.html). Most RAG dashboards report a number that sounds like success: “the right document was in the top 5.” That is partial recall : at least one relevant passage made it into the context. Real questions rarely need one passage. They need a rule and the definition it depends on, or a limit and its exception. If retrieval finds one of the two, the model writes a confident answer from half the evidence, and a hit-rate metric scores it as a success. The metric that catches this is complete-evidence recall . For a question q with evidence spans E(q) and an assembled context C(q) : partial(q) = 1 if ∃ e ∈ E(q) : e ⊆ C(q) complete(q) = 1 if ∀ e ∈ E(q) : e ⊆ C(q) Between mid-September and the end of October 2026, several papers attacked this gap from the chunking side. Some optimise chunk boundaries directly, some follow the document’s own structure, and some build a graph over chunks. I implemented the core idea of each one in plain JavaScript and added them as a new page to my browser-native Advanced Local RAG demo : the Chunking Lab . Chuking Lab Live! Everything runs in your tab. There is no server, no API key and no model download. Retrieval is BM25 only, so every number in this post is deterministic and reproducible from a URL. A full run (parse, five chunkers, two retrieval modes, all metrics) takes about 11 ms in Node 22. The research QESChunker ( arXiv 2610.36557 , Oct 27) treats chunking as supervised optimisation. Given question–evidence (QE) pairs, human-written or LLM-generated, it picks the chunk boundaries that maximise how much evidence ends up retrievable. Without overlap, the objective decomposes over chunks and dynamic programming finds the exact optimum in polynomial time. With overlap, the objective is monotone submodular. Exact optimisation is then NP-hard, but greedy selection comes with a (1 − 1/√e) approximation guarantee. StrucChunk ( arXiv 2610.26313 , Oct 19) uses the structure the author already wrote. It treats a document as a graph of provisions, never cuts across a clause boundary, resolves cross-references (“see Section 4.2”) before embedding , and fuses BM25 with dense retrieval through Reciprocal Rank Fusion. On LegalBench-RAG, Char-Recall@8 goes from 23.59% to 48.18%. On one corpus, Recall@5 rises from 0.557 to 0.804, and the authors attribute 88% of that gain to chunking alone. SpectRAG ( arXiv 2610.36991 , Oct 27) stops treating chunks as independent. It builds a weighted graph over chunks (adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citations), seeds it from hybrid search, propagates relevance, and assembles a context under a fixed token budget . The goal is a context that is relevant, diverse, connected and sufficient. The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading ( arXiv 2610.26951 , Oct 18) supplies the diagnosis. Across ten frontier and three open-weight models, retrieval reliably surfaces some of the relevant chunks but not all of the chunks a multi-fact question needs. Chunking also strips the document-level context that resolves references between passages. Three September papers frame the rest: Pre-retrieval Query Clustering for Adaptive Top-k ( arXiv 2609.13489 ) picks retrieval depth per query cluster, reporting over 36% better F1 and 14% fewer tokens on easy clusters. Context size is a per-query variable. Parser, Chunking, and Embedding Interactions ( arXiv 2609.31660 ) runs a 54-configuration factorial study and finds parser and chunker choices interact, with no single retriever winning everywhere. Re-ranking and Late Interaction Drive Retrieval Quality ( arXiv 2609.38473 ) compares six pipelines over about 464,000 papers and finds the biggest levers after first-stage retrieval. The main demo already has a cross-encoder reranker for that. The test bed The corpus is a…

articles.title: Concurrency Programming (8): Read-Write Locks — From Language Rules to the CPU
articles.content: 0. What Does This Article Answer Next? The previous article ended by returning to Mutex: it protects an entire critical section, but it allows only one execution unit to enter at a time, regardless of whether that unit reads or writes. If two threads only read shared state, they do not need to block each other: Thread A Thread B read counter read counter A read-write lock refines Mutex by distinguishing Readers from Writers : This article continues with the same two examples: counter++ to see how the Write Lock provides Atomicity; counter + ready to see how Write Lock → Read Lock establishes Visibility and Ordering. As before, we start with the language-level rules, then trace how the JDK, HotSpot, and the CPU implement them. 1. What Does Java ReadWriteLock Guarantee at the Language Level? 1.1 Atomicity Java's ReadWriteLock defines the Reader / Writer boundary directly: “The read lock may be held simultaneously by multiple reader threads, so long as there are no writers.” It also states: “The write lock is exclusive.” Reads may therefore proceed concurrently, while writes remain exclusive. Use the same counter++ example: ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); Lock writeLock = rw.writeLock(); writeLock.lock(); try { counter++; } finally { writeLock.unlock(); } With two threads updating concurrently: Initial: counter = 0 Thread A Thread B writeLock.lock() writeLock.lock() wait read counter -> 0 counter + 1 -> 1 write counter -> 1 writeLock.unlock() writeLock.lock() returns read counter -> 1 counter + 1 -> 2 write counter -> 2 writeLock.unlock() The final value is: counter = 2 As with Mutex, Atomicity comes from serializing conflicting critical sections under the Write Lock , not from turning counter++ itself into an atomic instruction. A Read Lock should protect reads only. Multiple Readers may enter together, so it cannot be used to protect shared writes. 1.2 Visibility and Ordering ReadWriteLock also defines memory synchronization between the Write Lock and the associated Read Lock: “A thread successfully acquiring the read lock will see all updates made upon previous release of the write lock.” Use the same counter / ready example: int counter = 0; boolean ready = false; ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); Lock readLock = rw.readLock(); Lock writeLock = rw.writeLock(); // Thread A writeLock.lock(); try { counter = 1; ready = true; } finally { writeLock.unlock(); } // Thread B readLock.lock(); try { if (ready) { System.out.println(counter); } } finally { readLock.unlock(); } If B successfully acquires the Read Lock after A releases the Write Lock: By happens-before: So once B has acquired the subsequent Read Lock and observes ready == true, the earlier counter = 1 must be visible. This outcome is not allowed: ready == true counter == 0 That gives us two guarantees: Visibility : writes completed by the Writer before releasing the Write Lock are visible to a later Reader that acquires the Read Lock; Ordering : the Writer's writes, Write Lock release, Read Lock acquisition, and the Reader's reads form a happens-before order. 2. How Does the JDK Implement ReentrantReadWriteLock? 2.1 Layers Start with the implementation stack: 2.2 End-to-End Path from Write Lock to Read Lock Continue with counter / ready: Thread A writes under the Write Lock, then Thread B reads under the Read Lock. The sequence diagram keeps only the cross-layer path. The Runtime / Language Implementation layer can be expanded into the Reader / Writer contention flow below: Two counters are encoded in the synchronization state: In JDK 25, ReentrantReadWriteLock.Sync extends AbstractQueuedLongSynchronizer. Readers use Shared mode; Writers use Exclusive mode; both ultimately contend on the same 64-bit state. articles.title: Fire IT Consultancies: Regulated AI Demands Forward-Deployed Teams
articles.content: Generic offshore developers lack the deep architectural discipline required to ship compliant autonomous agents into production environments Legacy IT consultancies rely on brittle API wrappers, while Forward-Deployed Engineering requires precise architectural discipline to protect margins and compliance. The Production Breaking Point: Why Off-Site Delivery Fails in Regulated AI At 3:14 AM on a Thursday, the core credit underwriting pipeline of a Tier-1 financial institution suffered a catastrophic, silent implosion. A massive multi-agent system — hastily deployed by a generic offshore IT consultancy under a standard time-and-materials contract — had entered a state of Verification Collapse. Three autonomous agents, designated for document extraction, risk profiling, and compliance checking, failed to bound their reasoning logic. Instead of challenging contradictory data, the agents hallucinated a false consensus regarding a synthetic corporate financial history. Within eleven minutes, the system autonomously approved over 4,200 unauthorized commercial loan applications. Because the offshore developers relied on ephemeral context windows rather than durable state boundaries, the agents became trapped in a recursive retry loop, generating over 14,000 hidden reasoning tokens per request until an Out of Memory (OOM) error saturated the H100 cluster and crashed the primary inference pipeline. This was not a standard software bug to be triaged in a morning stand-up; it was an immediate kinetic balance-sheet escalation. The telemetry failure instantly breached strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs) under the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), translating to a $14.5M statutory liability and triggering emergency reporting protocols to sovereign regulators. The offshore vendor’s architectural naivety — specifically their inability to enforce deterministic state boundaries upon probabilistic models — had transformed an experimental cost-saving initiative into a material financial event. Legacy IT delivery models operate on the assumption that writing API wrappers around foundation models is equivalent to engineering systems. The reality of the transaction floor proved violently otherwise. 📊 Executive Summary: The transition from deterministic code to probabilistic agentic AI renders legacy IT consultancies dangerously obsolete. Deploying autonomous workflows into regulated enterprise data streams demands a new architectural discipline — Forward-Deployed Engineering. By mathematically enforcing state boundaries, utilizing zero-trust execution, and disaggregating inference topologies, FDEs eliminate the 20× token retry multiplier, slash Token COGS by up to 40%, and neutralize kinetic SLA and regulatory balance-sheet liabilities. The Structural Fallacy of Context Stuffing and Ephemeral State The architectural root cause of production AI failures invariably stems from the fundamental physics of attention mechanisms and a gross misunderstanding of working memory. Generic developers attempt to solve complex reasoning bottlenecks by indiscriminately stuffing 128K or 1 million tokens of enterprise data into a single prompt. This “context stuffing” strategy directly triggers the Positional Attention Paradox. Empirical telemetry demonstrates a severe U-shaped accuracy degradation curve: models with native 128K context windows frequently drop below 50% precision when extracting specific facts hidden in the middle 50% of the token span (Liu et al., 2023). A massive context window does not guarantee comprehension; it simply provides a larger middle ground where critical compliance data is functionally invisible to the model. Furthermore, standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) exhibits catastrophic O(L²) memory growth due to the full-resolution caching of high-dimensional key and value matrices. articles.content: Foldable phones still command a hefty investment, evident with recent releases like the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 that easily cost thousands of dollars. That’s why you should take into consideration the Motorola Razr (2025). Right now you can get the Motorola Razr (2025) for just $29 at Boost Mobile . Normally the flip-style phone costs $599, but it’s discounted down by $570 in this limited-time Black Friday deal that gives you all the benefits of a foldable phone, without cleaning out your wallet before the holidays even start. The Motorola Razr (2025) is a flip style phone with the utility that makes one-handed use and vlogging easier, thanks to how it pairs its dual rear cameras with its 3.6-inch outer screen. Boost Mobile discounts the phone to $29 when you prepay two months of unlimited service and port in an existing phone number. View Deal To get this incredible deal, there is a catch you need to know about: you must port in your existing phone number and prepay for two months of Boost Mobile’s Unlimited Premium plan. That plan runs $120 for the two-month period, which brings your out-of-pocket checkout total to $149.99 plus tax. Once you meet those two requirements, you get the Motorola Razr (2025) for just $29. Beyond running full apps, another major benefit is effortless one-handed use — you aren't stretching your fingers across a massive screen, making it ideal for subway commuters holding onto a handrail with the other hand. The main drawback of the Motorola Razr (2025) is its MediaTek Dimensity 7300X processor. Low-light photography can also be hit-or-miss compared to pricier flagships. Even so, snagging the Razr for $29 through Boost Mobile is a steal. While you are locked into paying for two months of premium service upfront, you can always drop down to a cheaper plan after the initial 60 days. articles.content: A prototype of Shield AI’s X-Bat AI fighter jet, which will be built in the Seattle area. (Photo via Shield AI) Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle. Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas. The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s. In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing. The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire. Related Shield AI selects Seattle area to build X-BAT autonomous fighter jet, plans to add 4,000 jobs by early 2030s “This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post . “That is no small feat.” San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September. It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare. “The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.” Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A. One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.” The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways. “Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.” Related Meet the X-BAT: Full specs on the new AI-piloted fighter jet to be built in Washington state Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million. Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng,…

articles.title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
articles.content: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise. This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs. About Indegene Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments. Why conventional data quality programs break down Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve. One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult. Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent. Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly. Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users…

articles.title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. The problem: Too many systems, too much friction U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. Reach : agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time. Depth : chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis. Community : a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division. The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year.…

articles.title: Google announces it will cut off internet search access for schools that reject AI
articles.content: Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to using artificial intelligence , the tech giant said Tuesday. The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom . On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off — including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI , schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search. “We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post. The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.” But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products. Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers. Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older. Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers. “Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.” New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use. Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically . And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development. Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products. “Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement. Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.” —Barbara Ortutay, AP Technology Writer

articles.title: Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change
articles.content: Ai2 plans to use funding from Google to build an open-source AI model for projecting climate change decades into the future. (Ai2 Image) Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future. The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years. Announced Wednesday morning , the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org , the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work. Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling. (LinkedIn Photo) Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer , Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling. “Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.” Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM , which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate. In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense. Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models. Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them. Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research. Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen , who started a climate modeling effort around 2016 at what was then known as Vulcan, his Seattle-based holding company. The group moved to Ai2 in 2021 , about two and a half years after his death. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014. The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem. In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.” Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models , called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet. Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change. The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems.
